question: A location where flammable vapors may be present in ignitible amounts during normal operation is:
explain_plain: Class I is gas and vapor, and Division 1 is the hazard present in normal operation. Class II is dust and Class III is fibers.

question: Class II locations are hazardous because of:
explain_plain: Class II is the combustible dust class. Gases and vapors are Class I, and fibers and flyings are Class III.

question: Class III, Division 1 covers areas where ignitible fibers or flyings are:
explain_plain: Class III splits differently: Division 1 is where fibers are handled, manufactured, or used, and Division 2 is storage and other handling. That split is why the Division 1 wording for Class III does not match Class I and II exactly.

question: Which of these is a protection technique listed for hazardous locations?
explain_plain: Explosionproof equipment is a listed technique, along with dust-ignitionproof, purging and pressurizing, oil immersion, nonincendive design, and intrinsic safety. Ordinary methods and boxes are not techniques at all.

question: Equipment approved for Division 1 of a class and group may be used in:
choices: Division 2 of the same class and group
Class II if it is Class I approved
Any group of the same class
explain_plain: Division approval flows downward only, and only inside the same class and group. Class or group approval never transfers on its own.

question: The wiring and equipment rules for Class I locations are in Article:
explain_plain: Article 501 is Class I, 502 is Class II dust, and 503 is Class III fibers. Occupancy articles send their classified areas back to 501.

question: In a major repair garage with no fuel dispensing, the floor area up to 18 inches is commonly classified as:
explain_plain: Gasoline vapor hugs the floor, so the low band in a major repair garage is Class I, Division 2 in the common table case. Pits are the more severe spaces, not the open floor band.

question: A parking garage with no repair work is:
explain_plain: Parking and storage garages are not required to be classified. Classification begins when repair work with flammable fuels begins.

question: A garage pit with the ventilation described in 511.3 is generally classified as:
explain_plain: Ventilation is what buys the pit down to Division 2. Without that ventilation the pit answer is Division 1.

question: Wiring inside a classified area of a commercial garage must comply with:
explain_plain: Section 511.4 sends classified garage areas to the Class I rules of Article 501. Ordinary cable articles do not govern inside the classified boundary.

question: Fixed luminaires over a classified garage area are tied to which height in the common cases of 511.7?
explain_plain: Twelve feet is the key dimension for fixed lighting over classified areas, traffic lanes, and vehicle strike zones. Below it, the enclosure and guarding conditions of the section apply.

question: GFCI protection in a commercial garage is required:
explain_plain: The 2020 wording of 511.12 points to 210.8(B), which broadened it past the old diagnostic and hand tool list. It applies whether or not the spot is classified.

question: If fuel is dispensed inside a repair garage, which article applies in addition to 511?
explain_plain: Motor fuel dispensing is Article 514 wherever it happens, including inside a garage. Hangars are 513, bulk storage is 515, and spray work is 516.

question: Part II of Article 517 applies to:
explain_plain: The wiring and grounding part applies to patient care spaces. Offices, corridors, and waiting rooms are outside it.

question: Which area is listed in 517.10(B) as outside Part II?
explain_plain: Immunization-only areas were added to the not-covered list, along with psychiatry, alternative medicine, and optometry areas. Treatment spaces stay covered.

question: A patient care branch circuit needs how many ground-fault return paths under 517.13?
choices: Two working together — the metal method plus an insulated copper conductor
explain_plain: Redundant grounding is the point of 517.13: the metal raceway or armor path plus an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor. Either path alone is only half the requirement.

question: The insulated copper grounding conductor in a patient care space is sized from:
explain_plain: Equipment grounding conductors are sized from Table 250.122 by the overcurrent device ahead of them. Ampacity tables do not size grounding conductors.

question: An isolated ground receptacle inside a patient care vicinity is:
explain_plain: Section 517.16 bars isolated ground receptacles in the patient care vicinity. Outside the vicinity they need their own insulated grounding conductor run as directed.

question: A Category 2 (general care) patient bed location needs at least how many receptacles in NEC 2020?
explain_plain: The 2020 edition sets eight receptacles minimum at each Category 2 bed location, on at least two branch circuits. Counting per room instead of per bed is the classic takeoff miss.

question: The life safety branch of a hospital essential system follows the rules of:
explain_plain: Section 517.26 applies Article 700 to the life safety branch except for the items it lists. That cross-reference is why Chapter 7 is linked from this chapter.

question: Article 518 applies to an assembly space designed for at least how many persons?
explain_plain: One hundred or more persons is the threshold in 518.1. Smaller assembly rooms are wired under the general chapters.

question: Which is a permitted fixed wiring method in an assembly occupancy under 518.4(A)?
choices: Type MC cable with an insulated grounding conductor
explain_plain: Metal raceways, concrete-encased nonmetallic raceways, and MI, MC, or AC cable are the listed family. NM cable is not a fixed method for the fire-rated assembly cases.

question: New section 518.6 (2020) requires what at electrical equipment serving an assembly occupancy?
choices: Illumination of the working space, not controlled by automatic means only
explain_plain: Working spaces serving assembly occupancies, including outdoors, need illumination that a timer or sensor alone cannot switch off. Existing nearby light that does the job can satisfy it.

question: GFCI protection under 547.5(G) is required for which receptacles?
choices: 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles in the listed areas
explain_plain: The 2020 clarification limits the barn GFCI list to 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles in equipotential plane areas, outdoors, damp or wet locations, and dirt confinement areas. Bigger receptacles are outside that list.

question: Livestock buildings on the same premises are supplied from:
explain_plain: Section 547.9 requires supply from a distribution point with a four-wire grounded arrangement. The layout keeps neutral current out of the earth and reduces stray voltage.

question: An equipotential plane is bonded to the building grounding system with solid copper of at least:
explain_plain: At least 8 AWG solid copper, with listed pressure connectors or clamps, bonds the plane in 547.10. The same 8 AWG figure appears for marina bonding in 555.13.

question: For a floating pier, the electrical datum plane is:
choices: 30 inches above the water and at least 12 inches above the deck
explain_plain: Both dimensions must be met at a floating pier: 30 inches above the water and at least 12 inches above the deck. Fixed facilities use their own datum cases in the same section.

question: Marina bonding of metal parts in contact with the water uses solid copper of at least:
explain_plain: Section 555.13 sets 8 AWG solid copper minimum for bonding back to the panelboard grounding bus. Undersizing the bond is a failed layer of the shock protection system.

question: A shore power disconnect (2020 numbering, 555.17) must be located within how far of its receptacle?
explain_plain: Not more than 30 inches, readily accessible, identified, and ahead of the receptacle. In NEC 2023 this moved to 555.36, which Florida has not adopted.

question: Marina receptacles (2020 numbering, 555.19) mount at least how far above the deck?
explain_plain: At least 12 inches above the deck surface, and never below the electrical datum plane. Deck replacement can change the finished height and must be rechecked.

question: Shore power receptacles get individual GFPE set to open at not more than:
explain_plain: Thirty milliamperes is the shore power GFPE ceiling in 555.35. Five milliamperes is personnel GFCI territory, and 100 milliamperes is the feeder level.

question: Feeder conductors supplying a dock or slip get GFPE set at not more than:
explain_plain: One hundred milliamperes is the feeder and branch level in 555.35(B). The shore receptacle level below it is 30 milliamperes.

question: Holiday decorative temporary installations are limited to:
explain_plain: Ninety days is the holiday and decorative limit in 590.3. Construction power instead lasts for the work itself and is removed when the work ends.

question: A temporary service installation must comply with:
explain_plain: Section 590.4(A) sends temporary services to Article 230. Temporary relaxes selected methods, not the service safety core.

question: On a construction site, receptacles may be installed on a branch circuit that supplies:
choices: Nothing else — receptacle circuits stay separate from temporary lighting
explain_plain: Section 590.4(D)(1) keeps receptacles off temporary lighting circuits so a receptacle fault cannot kill the lights. The separation is a worker safety rule, not a load rule.

question: Splices in temporary wiring must be:
choices: In a box or enclosure with a cover installed
explain_plain: Section 590.4(G) requires an enclosure with a cover for every splice. Open splices fail on temp work just as they do on permanent work.

question: Cable assemblies used as temporary feeders or branch circuits:
choices: May lie on the floor if heavy duty
May not be installed on the ground or floor
explain_plain: Section 590.4(J) bars feeder and branch circuit cables from the ground or floor, and 590.4(H) requires protection at doorways and pinch points. Extension cords used as cords are a different case.

question: GFCI protection under 590.6(A) covers which receptacles used for construction work?
choices: Only receptacles in the temp panel
explain_plain: The (A) list runs to 30-ampere receptacles and includes permanent building receptacles being used for the work. Everything else used for temporary power is covered by (B).

question: For receptacles outside the 590.6(A) list, the alternative to GFCI protection is:
choices: An assured equipment grounding conductor program
explain_plain: Section 590.6(B) allows GFCI protection or a documented assured grounding program with scheduled testing. A sign is not a protection method.

question: New section 590.8 (2020) addresses what in temporary installations?
choices: Overcurrent protective devices, including reused devices
explain_plain: Section 590.8 covers overcurrent devices in temp installations, including inspection and maintenance of reused devices and current-limiting cases. It targets the junk-drawer temp panel habit.

question: Before wiring a suspect area, the crew should work from:
choices: Their own judgment of what looks safe
explain_plain: Section 500.4 expects the classification, materials, and boundaries to be documented and available to those designing, installing, and inspecting. Guessing a classification is how ordinary methods end up inside classified boundaries.

question: The emergency disconnect at a motor fuel dispensing facility must:
choices: Disconnect all circuit conductors of the circuits served
Only stop the pump motor signal
explain_plain: The 2020 clarification to 514.11 requires disconnection of all circuit conductors, not a single leg. A partial disconnect leaves the dispenser partly alive in an emergency.

question: For ampacity, copper-clad aluminum (CCA) conductors are sized from:
choices: A separate CCA column in Table 310.16
explain_plain: Table 310.16's aluminum column covers aluminum and copper-clad aluminum,. That is why CCA runs one AWG size up from copper for the same breaker.

question: Which termination is permitted for a CCA branch-circuit conductor?
choices: A push-in backstab hole on a receptacle
explain_plain: Standard 15/20A device screw terminals accept CCA; splices and lugs must be marked AL/CU, CC, or CC-CU for the metals joined. Backstab holes are listed for 14 AWG solid copper only — never CCA.

question: A 10 AWG THHN CCA conductor and a 10 AWG THHN copper conductor in the same conduit:
choices: The CCA conductor counts double for fill
The copper conductor counts double for fill
They count exactly the same for conduit fill
CCA is not permitted in conduit
explain_plain: Conduit fill (Chapter 9 Tables 4 and 5) and box fill (314.16) are figured by conductor size and insulation type, not by the metal. Same AWG and insulation, same fill — the difference is only that CCA is chosen one size up for ampacity.

question: Chapter 9 Table 8 resistance values for voltage-drop calculations list:
choices: Copper and aluminum only — CCA needs cited manufacturer or UL data
explain_plain: Table 8 gives copper and aluminum properties; there is no CCA column. A CCA voltage-drop figure must come from cited manufacturer or UL data for the actual product, and stays flagged unverified until that data is on file.
